title: Likes and dislikes
goal: Express likes, dislikes, interests and opinions — and see why "like" in Danish takes three words.
bekal: use *jeg kan godt lide*, *jeg elsker*, *jeg hader*
talk about hobbies and free time
wave: Review **unit 14** first: make a shopping list of ten items with their measures, out loud, in Danish.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Hvad laver du i din fritid?
dialogs.intro: An afternoon in Fælledparken. Mette, Budi and Ahmad sit down after a game of soccer.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Budi, du er faktisk god til fodbold.
lines.id: Budi, you're actually good at soccer.
lines.literal: Budi, you are actually good at football.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tak! Jeg kan godt lide at spille. Men jeg er bedre til badminton.
lines.id: Thanks! I like playing. But I'm better at badminton.
lines.literal: thanks! I can well like to play. but I am better at badminton.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Badminton? Det er Danmarks nationalsport, næsten.
lines.id: Badminton? That's practically Denmark's national sport.
lines.literal: badminton? it is Denmark's national-sport, almost.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Det ved jeg. Indonesien og Danmark møder hinanden tit.
lines.id: I know. Indonesia and Denmark often play each other.
lines.literal: that know I. Indonesia and Denmark meet each-other often.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Hvad laver du ellers i din fritid?
lines.id: What else do you do in your free time?
lines.literal: what make you else in your free-time?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg elsker at lave mad. Og jeg hører meget musik.
lines.id: I love cooking. And I listen to a lot of music.
lines.literal: I love to make food. and I hear much music.

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jeg hader at lave mad. Jeg bestiller bare pizza.
lines.id: I hate cooking. I just order pizza.
lines.literal: I hate to make food. I order just pizza.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Det er dyrt i længden. Synes du ikke?
lines.id: That gets expensive in the long run. Don't you think?
lines.literal: it is expensive in length-the. think you not?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jo, men jeg tror ikke, jeg lærer det nogensinde.
lines.id: Sure, but I don't think I'll ever learn.
lines.literal: yes, but I believe not, I learn it ever.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jeg kan lære dig det. Kan du lide stærk mad?
lines.id: I can teach you. Do you like spicy food?
lines.literal: I can teach you it. can you like strong food?

lines.speaker: Ahmad:
lines.text: Jeg elsker stærk mad. Danskere kan slet ikke lide det.
lines.id: I love spicy food. Danes don't like it at all.
lines.literal: I love strong food. Danes can at-all not like it.

lines.speaker: Mette:
lines.text: Hey! Jeg kan godt lide chili. Bare ikke for meget.
lines.id: Hey! I do like chili. Just not too much.
lines.literal: hey! I can well like chili. just not too much.

notes: **Kan godt lide** is a three-word phrase that can't be split, and it's the only ordinary way to say "like" in Danish. Literally something like "can well bear" — it makes no sense taken apart, so don't. Learn it whole: *jeg kan godt lide*.
**To negate it, put ikke in the middle:** *jeg kan **ikke** lide* = I don't like. Notice *godt* disappears in the negative. To strengthen it: *jeg kan **slet ikke** lide* = I don't like it at all.
**God til** = good at. Always with *til*: *god til fodbold*, *god til dansk*, *dårlig til matematik*.
**Hinanden** = each other. *De møder hinanden* = they meet each other. Compare the *-s* form from unit 8 (*de mødes*) — both are correct and mean the same.

**Synes vs tror — don't mix them up.** *Jeg synes* expresses an **opinion** about something you've experienced yourself: *jeg synes, filmen er god* (I think the film is good). *Jeg tror* expresses a **guess** about something uncertain: *jeg tror, han kommer* (I think he's coming). English uses "think" for both; Danish doesn't. Using *tror* for an opinion sounds as if you're unsure of your own taste.
**I længden** = in the long run. A fixed phrase often heard in everyday arguments.
**Nogensinde** = ever (in negative sentences and questions). *Aldrig nogensinde* = never ever.
**Stærk mad** = spicy food — literally "strong food". Danish has no separate word for spicy. To check, ask: *Er det stærkt?*

grammars.title: Saying you like something: from hate to love
body: The full ladder, from bottom to top:

head: Phrase
Strength
Example
rows: Jeg hader at stå tidligt op.
Jeg kan slet ikke lide lakrids.
Jeg kan godt lide at cykle.
Jeg kan rigtig godt lide dansk mad.

after: After all these phrases, the next verb takes **at**: *jeg kan godt lide **at** spille*, *jeg elsker **at** rejse*. This is different from the modal verbs in unit 13, which take no *at*.
*Jeg er ligeglad med* literally means "I'm equally glad with" — in other words, I couldn't care less. Watch the tone: it can sound offhand or rude depending on how you say it.

**Lakrids** (licorice) is the Danish culture test. Danes eat it in earnest, including the salty kind (*salt lakrids*), and hardly any newcomer likes it on the first try. The sentence *jeg kan slet ikke lide lakrids* will come in very handy.

grammars.title: Synes, tror, ved, mener
body: Four verbs that can all be translated as "think" or "feel", but they can't be swapped for one another.

head: Verb
Used for
Example
rows: Jeg **ved**, at hun bor i Aarhus.
Han **mener**, at prisen er for høj.

after: ⚠️ *Jeg tror, filmen er god* sounds as if you haven't seen it yet. If you've seen it and liked it, the right word is *synes*.
*At tro* also means to believe in the religious sense: *Jeg tror på Gud.*
Notice they're all followed by a subordinate clause, and inside it the word order is different — *ikke* moves in front of the verb. The rule is in unit 20.

blocks.text: ⚠️ *At spille* is for games and musical instruments; *at lege* is for playing the way children do (without rules); *at dyrke* is for sports as a regular activity. Three words that are all "play" in English.
*At slappe af* = to relax, literally "to slacken off". The *af* part gets thrown to the end of the sentence like other phrasal verbs: *Jeg slapper **af** om aftenen.*

head: Dansk
English
rows: Det er jeg ikke enig i.

blocks.text: *Det kommer an på* is a four-word phrase that can't be split, just like *kan godt lide*. Learn it whole.

blocks.title: Tone when you disagree
items: Danes don't avoid disagreement and don't see it as impolite — calm debate is considered healthy. If you come from a culture that values harmony more, this can feel too direct at first.
But there's a limit: you attack the opinion, not the person. *Det er jeg ikke enig i* targets the idea; going after the person is still not acceptable.
A useful softener if you want to disagree gently: *Jeg kan godt se dit punkt, men…* ("I see your point, but…").

vocab.en: to be of the opinion; to mean

items: I don't like lakrids at all.
I think the film is good.
Jeg ____, at maden her er god. (you've tasted it)
Jeg ____, at han kommer klokken syv. (guess)
Jeg ____, det bliver koldt i morgen. (forecast)
Vi ____, at prisen er for høj. (opinion)

exercises.prompt: Put ikke in the right place. Write out the whole sentence.
Put the words in the right order.
items: fritid / laver / hvad / din / du / i / ?

answers: Jeg kan godt lide at spille badminton. — Jeg kan ikke lide kaffe. — Jeg elsker at lave mad. — Jeg kan slet ikke lide lakrids. — Jeg synes, filmen er god. — Jeg tror, det regner i morgen.
Jeg kan ikke lide kaffe. — Han elsker ikke at lave mad. — Jeg synes ikke, det er godt. — Vi spiller ikke fodbold om søndagen. — Jeg er ikke enig.
